newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: East European bourses nervous ahead of Fed meeting.
newsitem.headline: East European bourses nervous ahead of Fed meeting.

text.p: Worries about next week's meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve overshadowed central and eastern European share markets this week, with only Romania showing much sign of life.

With markets in East and West concerned that the U.S. central bank might raise interest rates, the main exception in the region was Bucharest where two unofficial indices soared 15 percent. This was due to local investors' expectations of a depreciation of the Romanian currency.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25 to discuss interest rates and some analysts believe it will raise them in a pre-emptive strike against inflation.
A rate rise could make booming Western markets tumble and send shock waves into already fragile markets in post-communist Europe.
WARSAW
Shares on the Warsaw Stock Exchange fell this week in profit-taking with analysts saying that they were braced for more losses driven by fears of a U.S. rate rise and labour protests in Poland.
Some analysts said the slide, which started last week, was caused by retail players taking profits after a 30-percent surge since early 1997.
They said large players kept on the sidelines waiting for better bargains and could step in and start buying when the bourse slips to about 15,500.
Construction firm Espebepe plunged 46.4 percent this week on mounting concern that the firm would go bankrupt.
The mood was generally more optimistic for the longer term with analysts citing the underlying strength of the Polish economy as evidence that the Warsaw market remained a good long-term investment.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian shares moved in directionless trade throughout the week, indicating investor uncertainty before the U.S. Fed meeting and an absence of corporate news.
"A rate hike in the U.S. may have a knock-on effect on the emerging markets," one trader said.
The Hungarian market received little support from the domestic corporate side as companies prepare for their annual shareholders' meetings in April, traders said.
PRAGUE
The PX50 index on the Prague bourse showed the first glimmerings of an upturn in mid-week but falls from the major issues on Friday pulled the PX50 back down.
Dealers blamed the absence of foreign buying for losses to the index's three most heavily capitalised shares.
"For me it looks like we're still missing interest from foreign investors," said Ivan Kusacek of Zivnostenska Banka.
On Friday, SPT Telecom dropped 35 crowns to 3,410, CEZ fell 13 crowns to 1,062 and Komercni Banka also lost ground, falling 12 crowns to 2,443.
Together the shares account for 45 percent of the PX50's capitalisation and often have a decisive influence on the direction of the market.
BUCHAREST
Turnover on the Bucharest bourse rose to around six billion lei in the week's three trading sessions from some 4.7 billion last week as buying pressure started to mount.
Traders said an expected depreciation of the Romanian currency sent local investors rushing to buy shares.
High-caps Oltchim chemical plant and fertiliser maker Azomures dominated the exchange, taking more than 90 percent of each session's turnover.
Demand for the other 24 stocks, listed on the second tier, was light.
BRATISLAVA
Slovak blue chips continued to rise on the Bratislava Stock Exchange this week but brokers said the growth appeared fragile, and was made on generally small volumes.

"The general sluggish sentiment on the world markets now appears to have infiltrated the Slovak bourse, putting many foreign investors on the sidelines as they await a stronger impulse to show the bourse's future trend," said Radovan Dzugas of Creditanstalt.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks extended their losses at the end of the week with analysts predicting price stability in the next two weeks.
They said investors, particularly foreigners, were holding back but expected some shares to rebound slightly after having hit rock bottom.
Fully-listed drugs firm Pliva closed 15 kuna lower at 425 kuna than a week ago, but was seen recovering shortly.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell five percent this week, as the blue-chip SBI index fell 69.75 points to 1,321.24.
CESI
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 73 Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian shares, lost 0.9 percent to 1,526.6.
